idea.title: Nice was an insult
idea.summary: The word nice meant foolish when English borrowed it from French, and slowly turned into a compliment; closes on saying nice to meet you to a stranger.
hookOptions: You say nice all day. It was an insult.
I called him nice. In 1290 that was rude.
The nicest word in English started as an insult
sources: Etymonline 'nice': late 13c., 'foolish, stupid, senseless', from Old French nice 'silly, foolish', from Latin nescius 'ignorant', from nescire 'not know'.
Etymonline 'nice': meaning shifted over centuries, with senses like 'kind, thoughtful' by the 1700s (Merriam-Webster also notes the shift from foolish to pleasant).

scenes.say: The word nice used to mean stupid.
In the 1200s, English borrowed it from French, where it meant silly or foolish.
The root is Latin, nescius, which means ignorant.
For centuries it was an insult, until the 1700s, when it slowly turned kind.

scenes.name: Cheeky Lemon
scenes.say: So when you tell a stranger nice to meet you, that word changed sides.
Go say it to someone new.
